title: Boiling point elevation with a partially dissociated solute: finding the mole percent dissociated
summary: Type the data from the question into the instrument panel, press Run experiment, and watch the bench boil the pure solvent, dissolve B, fall short of your measurement, and then break B apart until the flask matches - the mole percent dissociated is the outcome of the run, not a printed calculation.
subject: Chemistry
topic: Elevation of boiling point with a partially dissociated solute
subtopics: Ebullioscopic constant from enthalpy of vaporisation
van't Hoff factor from dissociation stoichiometry
Cancellation of an unknown molar mass
concepts: Kb is not a table value here - it follows from the solvent's boiling point and enthalpy of vaporisation
Quoting the enthalpy of vaporisation as 10R makes the gas constant cancel out of Kb entirely
Kb is proportional to the solvent's molar mass and the molality is inversely proportional to it, so their product is independent of the solvent
A colligative property counts particles, so B giving 2C + 2D contributes four particles for every one that dissociates
i = 1 + 3(alpha) for B into 2C + 2D, bounded by 1 and 4
The rise in boiling point is measured from the pure solvent, not the boiling point itself
formulas: Kb = R (Tb0)^2 M_S / dHvap, with M_S in kg per mol
Kb = 16 M_S when Tb0 = 400 K and dHvap = 10R (M_S in g per mol)
m = mass of solute / (molar mass x mass of solvent in kg)
m = 0.25 / M_S for 0.25 % m/m with M_B = 10 M_S
Kb x m = 4.000 K, independent of the solvent

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: Kb from the thermodynamic definition, the molality from the mass percent, i from the measured rise and alpha from the dissociation stoichiometry

The cancellation of the solvent's molar mass checked symbolically with M_S carried as a free symbol - Kb x m reduces to the constant 4 K, so the result holds for every solvent and not merely for the values tried
Back-substitution with M_S = 12, 20, 33.3, 58.5 and 180 g/mol: alpha = 1/3 returns dTb = 8.000000 K and a boiling point of exactly 408 K in every case

Limiting cases: i = 1 + 3 alpha gives i = 1 at alpha = 0 and i = 4 at alpha = 1, bracketing boiling points of 404 K and 416 K, so the measured 408 K is consistent with partial dissociation as the question states
Units confirmed by dimensional analysis: K kg/mol times mol/kg leaves kelvin, and i is dimensionless

The distractors reproduced deliberately: i = 1 + alpha gives 100 %, which the word 'partially' rules out; ignoring dissociation gives 404 K; using Tb in place of dTb gives i = 102, above the ceiling of 4; ignoring the factor of ten in M_B gives a rise of 80 K. None is 33.33

The alternative reading of '0.25 % (mass/mass)' quantified rather than assumed: taking 0.25 g of B in 100 g of solution gives Kb x m = 4.0100 K, i = 1.99500 and 33.17 %. The paper's numbers are chosen so the conventional reading lands on i = 2 exactly and a clean 33.33, which is the intended answer

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which follows the same route (Kb = 16 M_S, Kb x m = 4, i = 2, i = 1 + 3 alpha) and reports the same 33.33. IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable at the time of writing

The chemistry and the answer are unchanged.

interactivity: Enter the data, run the experiment, watch it produce the answer: the page has three phases - an instrument panel you fill in, a run you watch step by step, and a result read off the finished run

Seven input boxes, one for every quantity the question gives: the boiling point of the pure solvent, the enthalpy of vaporisation as a multiple of R, the molar-mass ratio of B to S, the concentration in mass percent, the boiling point of the solution, and the two stoichiometric coefficients of B into C and D
There is deliberately no box for the molar mass of the solvent, because the experiment does not need one - section 03 proves it
Every entry is validated as it is typed, with the reason given in place; the Run experiment button stays disabled until all seven boxes hold usable values
Nothing is precomputed: the model runs on whatever is entered, so the page reaches a different answer for different data and refuses data that cannot be reconciled

The run has six visible steps on a rail, each narrated in terms of the numbers the student typed: boil the pure solvent, weigh in B, boil again, compare with the measurement, let B dissociate, count what is left
Step 1 fills the flask, the hotplate glows, bubbles start and the thermometer climbs to the entered boiling point of the pure solvent - the baseline everything else is measured from
Step 2 drops twelve drawn units of B into the liquid and the molality appears in the working
Step 3 boils the solution with nothing dissociated and lands short of the measurement, which is the whole point of the question made visible
Step 4 draws the shortfall as an orange band on the temperature scale, labelled with the kelvin nobody has accounted for yet

Step 5 lets B break apart: each unit visibly comes apart into two C and two D, the particle count climbs, and the thermometer rises with it until it reaches the measurement the student entered - the answer emerges from the run rather than being printed
Step 6 counts what is in the flask - twelve dissolved, twenty-four present - and that ratio is the van't Hoff factor
Six live gauges that fill in only as the run establishes them, with the mole percent staying blank until the final step
The working is written one line at a time as the step that earns it is carried out, and the box scrolls itself to the newest line
A chart of boiling point against mole percent dissociated, drawn from the entered data, with the measurement dashed across it and a marker that travels along the curve during step 5
Playback controls: pause, resume, replay, and 0.5x / 1x / 2x speed, plus a change-the-data button that returns to the instrument panel with the entries kept
The result panel gives the answer with a plain-language account of how the run produced it, quoting the student's own numbers at every stage

The bench refuses impossible data and says why: a boiling point below the undissociated value, or above the ceiling that complete dissociation could reach, stops the run at the comparison step with the ceiling stated
Entering one C and one D reproduces the commonest wrong reading, 100 percent, as a run rather than as a warning
A separate panel sweeps the molar mass of the solvent across its whole range and shows Kb rising, the molality falling and their product never moving - computed from the data the student entered
A log of every run made, refusals included, and a lab notebook that writes itself when the bench settles something
A record of the run that fills in quantity by quantity, four cards on the wrong answers this question really produces, and the derivation gated until a run finishes
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log
